## Housekeeping/setup {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                  # installer for packages the browser lacks
await micropip.install("seaborn")                # fetch seaborn; first run takes a few seconds

import numpy as np                               # arrays and arithmetic (Module 3)
import pandas as pd                              # tables (Module 4)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                  # the base plotting layer
import seaborn as sns                            # statistical figures built on matplotlib

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # 67 counties, CDC PLACES 2024
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region, urbanicity, metro, population
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"],     # attach county attributes by key
                      how="left")                          # keep every asthma row

print(joined.shape)                              # rows, columns: expect (67, 11)
```

## Graphics in Python {.smaller}

Summarising data, numerically or graphically, is a central part of any analysis. Three layers
produce figures in Python:

1\. **matplotlib** — the original plotting library. Every figure in Python is ultimately a
matplotlib figure.

2\. **pandas `.plot()`** — a shortcut that calls matplotlib directly from a DataFrame.

3\. **seaborn** — statistical figures built on matplotlib: it takes a DataFrame and column
names, and handles grouping, colour, and legends.

This module begins with matplotlib, which every other layer depends on, and then turns to
seaborn. Module 6 continues with seaborn's statistical layers, facets, scales, and themes.

::: {.notes}
This is the Python counterpart of the "three graphics systems" slide in the R half, and the
mapping is close: matplotlib is base R graphics, seaborn is the closest thing Python has to
ggplot2, and pandas `.plot()` sits in between.

The reason to start with matplotlib rather than skip straight to seaborn is practical. seaborn
draws on a matplotlib axes, and every time a seaborn figure needs a title, a label, a tick, or
a saved file, the call that does it is a matplotlib call. Learning seaborn without matplotlib
means being stuck the first time a default needs changing.

If someone has used ggplot2 in the R half and asks whether Python has a grammar-of-graphics
library: yes, `seaborn.objects`, and also `plotnine`, which copies ggplot2 almost line for line.
Neither is what most Python code in the wild uses, which is why the course teaches the
function interface.
:::

## The asthma data {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
print(asthma.head())                                       # first five rows
print()                                                    # blank line between outputs
print(asthma["asthma_prev_pct"].agg(["min", "max"]))       # the range across 67 counties
```

Source: CDC PLACES 2024, model-based estimates for adults, all 67 Pennsylvania counties.

**Adult asthma prevalence runs from 9.7% to 11.6%. The entire state fits inside two
percentage points.**

::: {.callout-important}
## The question this module opens
A variable that hardly varies looks like a dead end. What else moves with it?
:::

::: {.notes}
Put the range on the board and let it sit. Nine point seven to eleven point six. If you had
asked the room to guess first, half of them would have said some county runs at twenty-five
percent and another at three.

The instinct when a variable does not vary is to conclude there is nothing here. That instinct
is wrong often enough to be worth breaking today. A flat variable is not a boring variable — it
is one whose signal is somewhere other than its own spread.

There is a real reason this one is flat, and a student will ask. These are modelled small-area
estimates, built by borrowing strength across areas, and that smooths county differences by
construction. Part of the flatness is asthma; part of it is the estimator.

Do not answer the question yet. The last section of today answers it with a number, and the
figures in between are how the room gets there. Say also, once, that this course describes and
does not infer — no p-values, no tests — and that it will matter at the end.
:::

# matplotlib: the base layer {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## Every matplotlib figure is two objects {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                  # the plotting interface

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))           # create a canvas and one plotting area

print(type(fig))                                 # Figure: the whole canvas
print(type(ax))                                  # Axes: one set of coordinates on it
```

1\. The **figure** is the canvas: its size, its resolution, and the file it saves to

2\. The **axes** is one set of coordinates drawn on that canvas: the data, labels, and ticks

`plt.subplots()` returns both, and nearly every figure in practice begins with that call.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `ax` is not "axis"
An **axes** is an entire plotting area. An **axis** is one of its edges, reached as
`ax.xaxis` or `ax.yaxis`. The naming is unfortunate and permanent.
:::

::: {.notes}
Draw this on the board once and it stops being confusing for the rest of the course. The figure
is a sheet of paper. The axes is one chart drawn on that sheet. A sheet can hold four charts,
which is what multi-panel figures are, and Module 6 builds them.

The naming collision is genuinely bad. Axes-singular is the whole plot; axis is an edge.
Everyone trips on it, including people who have written matplotlib for a decade.

Two styles exist in the wild: `plt.plot()`, which draws on whatever axes is current, and
`ax.plot()`, which draws on the axes named. This course uses `ax.` for everything, because it is
the style that survives a second panel and the one where the code says where the thing is going.
:::

## Scatterplots {.smaller}

Examines the relationship between two numeric variables.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # canvas and one axes
ax.scatter(x=asthma["smoking_prev_pct"],                   # horizontal position: smoking
           y=asthma["asthma_prev_pct"])                    # vertical position: asthma
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

matplotlib receives **columns**, not column names. A bare name is an undefined variable:

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                  # plotting

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 2))           # canvas and one axes
ax.scatter(x=smoking_prev_pct,                   # a bare name: Python looks for a variable
           y=asthma_prev_pct)                    # NameError: name 'smoking_prev_pct' is not defined
```

::: {.notes}
Run the first cell and read the axes aloud in the order that matters. Smoking runs across about
eleven points, from ten and a half to nearly twenty-two. Asthma runs across two. The cold open
said asthma barely moves; this picture is the first hint of what it moves with. Do not give the
number yet.

Then run the second cell and let it fail on the projector. This is the same mistake the R half
shows with `plot(x = bwt, y = age)`: the column lives inside the DataFrame, and Python has no
way to know that. The error names the missing variable, which is the clue — the fix is
`asthma["smoking_prev_pct"]`.

Notice there are no labels on the first figure. That is on purpose; the build-up later in the
session adds them one step at a time.
:::

## Histograms {.smaller}

A graphical summary of the distribution of one numeric variable. `bins` sets the number of bins,
or their exact edges.

```{pyodide}
import numpy as np                                         # evenly spaced bin edges
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
prev = asthma["asthma_prev_pct"]                           # the column to summarise

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3))    # two panels side by side
left.hist(prev)                                            # default: 10 bins, edges set by the data
left.set_title("Default bins")                             # panel title

edges = np.linspace(9.6, 11.8, 12)                         # 11 bins of width 0.2, on round numbers
right.hist(prev, bins=edges,                               # explicit bin edges
           color="#003594", edgecolor="white")             # fill colour; white gaps between bars
right.set_title("Bins of 0.2 points")                      # panel title
right.set_xlabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")            # x-axis label with units
right.set_ylabel("Number of counties")                     # y-axis label

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
The default is a guess by the library, not a finding. Ten bins, with edges wherever the minimum
and maximum happen to put them — here 9.89, 10.08, 10.27, numbers nobody would choose. The right
panel sets the edges on round numbers with `np.linspace`, which is the Python version of R's
`seq()` inside `breaks`.

Read the shape, because it is the cold open restated. Everything piles up between ten and eleven
and a half. Nothing is out in a tail.

Bin choice is a real decision and worth thirty seconds of live editing. Change 12 to 4 and the
structure disappears into a block; change it to 40 and every county gets its own spike.

Contrast with a bar chart now, so it sticks later: a histogram's x-axis is a number line, the
order is fixed by arithmetic, and the bars touch because the bins are adjacent intervals.
:::

## Histograms + reference lines {.smaller}

A second layer drawn on the same axes. `ax.axvline()` adds a vertical line at a value.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
prev = asthma["asthma_prev_pct"]                           # the column to summarise

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
ax.hist(prev, bins=12,                                     # layer 1: the histogram
        color="#003594", edgecolor="white")                # fill and bar edges
ax.axvline(prev.mean(), color="#8a6400",                   # layer 2: a line at the mean
           linestyle="--", linewidth=2,                    # dashed, thicker than default
           label=f"Mean {prev.mean():.2f}")                # legend text
ax.axvline(prev.median(), color="#6b7280",                 # layer 3: a line at the median
           linestyle=":", linewidth=2,                     # dotted, so it differs from the mean
           label=f"Median {prev.median():.2f}")            # legend text
ax.set_xlabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # x-axis label
ax.set_ylabel("Number of counties")                        # y-axis label
ax.legend(frameon=False)                                   # legend from each layer's label=
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
Every call to `ax.` adds a layer to the same axes, in the order the lines run. That is the whole
idea of layering, and it is the same idea the R half uses when it adds a density curve on top of
a histogram. Module 6 does the density curve properly with seaborn.

The two numbers are 10.66 and 10.60. Mean and median sitting this close says the distribution is
roughly symmetric, with no tail dragging the mean. When those two lines separate on a figure, the
mean is being pulled and the median is the more honest summary.

`label=` on each layer is what `ax.legend()` reads. No label, no legend entry. That is the
matplotlib habit to build: name the layer when you draw it.
:::

## Boxplots {.smaller}

A graphical summary of a distribution: the **median**, the **interquartile range** (the box), and
the spread beyond it (the whiskers).

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

levels = ["Metro", "Nonmetro"]                             # the two groups, in display order
groups = [joined.loc[joined["metro"] == m,                 # rows in group m ...
                     "asthma_prev_pct"]                    # ... asthma column only
          for m in levels]                                 # one Series per group

fig, (one, by) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))      # two panels
one.boxplot(joined["asthma_prev_pct"])                     # a single distribution
one.set_xticks([1], ["All 67 counties"])                   # boxes sit at x = 1, 2, ...
one.set_ylabel("Adult asthma prevalence (%)")              # y-axis label

by.boxplot(groups)                                         # one box per Series in the list
by.set_xticks([1, 2], levels)                              # name the boxes
by.set_xlabel("Metro status")                              # x-axis label

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
The line is the median, the box holds the middle half of the counties, the whiskers reach the
furthest points within one and a half box-lengths, and anything beyond that is drawn as a single
point. Four numbers and a picture in one glance. Make sure that is understood rather than nodded
at, because Module 6 leans on it.

The grouped version is where matplotlib shows its age. In R the formula `bwt ~ smoke` does the
split; here the split is a list comprehension, one Series per group, and the labels go on by
hand. That clumsiness is the honest motivation for seaborn, which does the split from a column
name. Do not apologise for it — show it once, then promise the shortcut.

Read the right panel: the boxes overlap almost entirely. Nonmetro sits a touch higher, 10.7
against 10.5 at the median. Metro status barely separates asthma. Keep that in mind for the end.
:::

## Pairs plots {.smaller}

`pd.plotting.scatter_matrix()` draws every pairwise scatter among several numeric columns, with a
histogram of each column on the diagonal.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
short = asthma.rename(columns={                            # short names fit the panel edges
    "asthma_prev_pct": "Asthma",                           # adult asthma (%)
    "smoking_prev_pct": "Smoking",                         # adult smoking (%)
    "obesity_prev_pct": "Obesity"})                        # adult obesity (%)

pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(short[["Asthma", "Smoking", "Obesity"]],  # three columns, 3 x 3 grid
                           figsize=(7, 4.6),               # canvas size in inches
                           diagonal="hist",                # histograms on the diagonal
                           color="#003594", alpha=0.7)     # point colour and transparency
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

Most useful for a handful of numeric columns.

::: {.notes}
This is R's `pairs()`. Nine panels, and the useful ones are the three below the diagonal — the
three above are the same scatters with the axes swapped.

Read the bottom-left region with the room. Asthma against smoking rises clearly. Asthma against
obesity rises, more loosely. Smoking against obesity rises too. Three variables, all moving
together to different degrees, which is exactly the situation where reading one scatter alone
can mislead.

The rename is not cosmetic. The panel edges are tiny, and `smoking_prev_pct` printed down the
side of a small panel is unreadable. Short names for a figure, long names in the data — that
split is worth adopting.

Pairs plots get unreadable past five or six columns. They are a first look, not a figure for a
report.
:::

# seaborn and the grammar of graphics {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## The grammar of graphics and seaborn {.smaller}

A statistical figure is assembled from independent components (Wilkinson, 2005):

1\. **Data** — a table, one row per observation

2\. **Mappings** — which column drives which visual property: position, colour, shape, size

3\. **A mark** — the geometric object that represents each row: a point, a line, a bar

In seaborn, the **function name is the mark** (`scatterplot`, `lineplot`, `countplot`), `data=`
names the table, and every mapping is a keyword that takes a **column name**.

```python
sns.scatterplot(data=joined,                # data
                x="smoking_prev_pct",       # mapping: column -> horizontal position
                y="asthma_prev_pct",        # mapping: column -> vertical position
                hue="metro")                # mapping: column -> colour
```

::: {.notes}
This is the idea the R half calls the grammar of graphics, and it is the same idea here, packaged
differently. In ggplot2 the mark is a separate layer you add with `+ geom_point()`. In seaborn the
mark is fused into the function name. The data and the mappings are the same concepts with the
same names.

The difference from matplotlib is the one to underline. matplotlib took columns —
`asthma["smoking_prev_pct"]`. seaborn takes a DataFrame and column *names*, as strings, and does
the lookup itself. That one change is why grouping becomes a single argument rather than a list
comprehension.

This block is plain code, not a live cell; it is the anatomy, and the next slides run it.
:::

## Goal {.smaller}

Build the following figure with seaborn, one component at a time.

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
# Drawn with matplotlib alone so it appears on page load; the build-up reproduces it in seaborn.
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))                   # canvas and one axes
for group, colour, marker in [("Metro", "#003594", "o"),   # one layer per group, with the
                              ("Nonmetro", "#8a6400", "X")]:  # colour and marker seaborn uses
    rows = joined[joined["metro"] == group]                # counties in this group
    ax.scatter(rows["smoking_prev_pct"],                   # smoking -> x
               rows["asthma_prev_pct"],                    # asthma -> y
               color=colour, marker=marker, s=50,          # group colour, shape, size
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.75,          # white rim, as seaborn draws it
               label=group)                                # legend entry
ax.set(title="Asthma against smoking, 67 Pennsylvania counties",   # title
       xlabel="Adult smoking prevalence (%)",              # x-axis label with units
       ylabel="Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
ax.legend(title="Metro status")                            # legend with a title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
Show the target before building it, the way the R half does. Ask the room to name every
component they can see: two variables on two axes, points, colour, shape, a title, axis labels,
a legend with a title. Each of those is one step on the next five slides.

Do not interpret the figure yet. The point of this slide is the anatomy. The interpretation is
the last section of today.
:::

## First: an ordered categorical column {.smaller}

pandas sorts text alphabetically. When categories have a natural order, `pd.Categorical()` fixes
it, and every figure and table then follows that order.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # one row per county

print(sorted(counties["urbanicity"].unique()))             # default: alphabetical order

levels = (counties.sort_values("urbanicity_code")          # code 1 = most urban, 6 = most rural
                  ["urbanicity"].unique())                 # names in that order
counties["urbanicity"] = pd.Categorical(                   # convert text to a categorical
    counties["urbanicity"],                                # the column to convert
    categories=levels,                                     # the order to keep
    ordered=True)                                          # the order carries meaning

print(counties["urbanicity"].cat.categories.tolist())     # the stored order
```

::: {.notes}
This is the Python version of R's `factor()` with `levels`. The R half converts a 0/1 smoking
code into a labelled factor; this file already has labels, so the problem here is order.

Read the first printout. Alphabetical puts Large central metro, Large fringe metro, Medium metro,
Micropolitan, Noncore, Small metro — Small metro has drifted to the end, after the rural codes.
Any figure drawn from that order would run from city to countryside and then jump back to a small
city. The second printout runs one to six, most urban to most rural, which is the order the NCHS
scheme intends.

Once the column is categorical, seaborn's axes and legends follow the stored order without being
told. The counting slide near the end of this section uses exactly this.
:::

## Text ↔ Plot (1 of 5) {.smaller}

Start with an **empty axes**.

```{pyodide}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                  # figure and axes

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))       # a canvas with one empty plotting area
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                       # render it: nothing is mapped yet
```

Every figure starts here. The axes is primed to receive data, and nothing is drawn yet.

::: {.notes}
The R half starts with `ggplot(data = birthwt)`, an empty grey panel. This is the same moment.
An empty axes, default limits of zero to one, nothing on it.

It looks like nothing, and that is the point. Everything that follows is added to this object,
one call at a time.
:::

## Text ↔ Plot (2 of 5) {.smaller}

Start with an empty axes. **Using `joined`, map smoking to the x-axis and asthma to the y-axis.
Represent each county with a point.**

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # empty axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined,                               # data
                x="smoking_prev_pct",                      # mapping: smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # mapping: asthma -> y
                ax=ax)                                     # draw on this axes
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

`scatterplot` is the mark. `ax=ax` places it on the axes created above.

::: {.notes}
Two things happened at once here, and in ggplot2 they would be two steps: the mapping and the
mark. seaborn fuses them, so the moment you say which columns go where, the points appear.

Notice the axis labels. Nobody typed them; seaborn used the column names. That is a default, and
it is the first thing the build-up will replace.

`ax=ax` is the habit to install now. Without it seaborn draws on whatever axes is current, which
works until the day there are two panels.
:::

## Text ↔ Plot (3 of 5) {.smaller}

… Represent each county with a point. **Map metro status to the colour and the shape of each
point.**

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # empty axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined,                               # data
                x="smoking_prev_pct",                      # mapping: smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # mapping: asthma -> y
                hue="metro",                               # mapping: metro -> colour
                style="metro",                             # mapping: metro -> marker shape
                ax=ax)                                     # draw on this axes
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

`hue=` maps a column to colour; `style=` maps a column to marker shape. seaborn builds the legend.

::: {.notes}
Two keywords, and the figure now carries a third variable. Both name the same column, so colour
and shape say the same thing twice — which is deliberate, because a figure printed in greyscale
still separates the groups by shape.

The legend appeared on its own. That is the payoff of mappings: seaborn knows which column drove
which property, so it can explain the mapping without being asked.

The shapes are seaborn's defaults, a circle and a cross. The colours are defaults too, and the
last build-up step replaces them. Read the cloud quickly: the nonmetro crosses sit further
right. Rural counties smoke more. Park that.
:::

## Text ↔ Plot (4 of 5) {.smaller}

… Map metro status to the colour and shape of each point. **Title the figure and label both axes
with units.**

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # empty axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data; smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                hue="metro", style="metro",                # metro -> colour and shape
                ax=ax)                                     # draw on this axes
ax.set(title="Asthma against smoking, 67 Pennsylvania counties",   # title
       xlabel="Adult smoking prevalence (%)",              # x-axis label with units
       ylabel="Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

`ax.set()` sets several properties of the axes in one call.

::: {.callout-important}
## The minimum for any figure that leaves a notebook
An x-label with units, a y-label with units, and a title that states what is plotted.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the step people skip, and it is a matplotlib call, not a seaborn one. seaborn drew on the
axes; matplotlib labels it. That division of labour is permanent.

The callout is the rule worth remembering. An exploratory figure can stay unlabelled while it
lives in a notebook only you read. The moment it goes into a slide, a report, or an email, you
are no longer the reader, and `smoking_prev_pct` means nothing to someone who did not write the
merge.

`ax.set()` is shorthand for `ax.set_title()`, `ax.set_xlabel()`, `ax.set_ylabel()`, all at once.
Either works.
:::

## Text ↔ Plot (5 of 5) {.smaller}

… Title the figure and label both axes with units. **Replace the default colours and title the
legend.**

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

palette = {"Metro": "#003594",                             # one colour per group, by name
           "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"}                          # dark gold for nonmetro

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # empty axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data; smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                hue="metro", style="metro",                # metro -> colour and shape
                palette=palette,                           # colours for the hue groups
                s=50, ax=ax)                               # point size; target axes
ax.set(title="Asthma against smoking, 67 Pennsylvania counties",   # title
       xlabel="Adult smoking prevalence (%)",              # x-axis label with units
       ylabel="Adult asthma prevalence (%)")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                  # replace the column-name title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

This is the goal figure.

::: {.notes}
Two changes. The palette is a dictionary, group name to colour, which is worth preferring over a
list: with a list the colours attach in whatever order seaborn meets the groups, and a filtered
table can silently swap them between two figures in the same report. With a dictionary, Metro is
royal blue every time.

The legend title was the column name, `metro`. `ax.get_legend()` reaches the legend seaborn built
and `.set_title()` replaces its title. Same pattern as before: seaborn builds, matplotlib adjusts.

Compare the code to the goal slide. It is identical. Five steps, each one sentence of the
description longer, and each one a line or two of code.
:::

## seaborn calls {.smaller}

`data` is seaborn's first argument and its name can be omitted. pandas `.plot.scatter()` draws
the same mark from the DataFrame itself.

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county

fig, (a, b, c) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 2.8))     # three panels

sns.scatterplot(data=asthma, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data named explicitly
                y="asthma_prev_pct", ax=a)                 # mappings; first panel
a.set_title("sns, data=asthma")                            # panel title

sns.scatterplot(asthma, x="smoking_prev_pct",              # data passed by position
                y="asthma_prev_pct", ax=b)                 # mappings; second panel
b.set_title("sns, data by position")                       # panel title

asthma.plot.scatter(x="smoking_prev_pct",                  # pandas: the DataFrame draws itself
                    y="asthma_prev_pct", ax=c)             # same columns; third panel
c.set_title("pandas .plot.scatter()")                      # panel title

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

The mappings `x=` and `y=` must always be named.

::: {.notes}
Three spellings, one figure. The R half shows the same thing: `ggplot(data = birthwt, ...)`,
`ggplot(birthwt, ...)`, and the pipe.

The pandas version is the fastest route during exploration, especially straight after a
`groupby` — `.plot.bar()` on a grouped Series is one line. It hands back a matplotlib axes, so
every `ax.set()` call still works on it. Nothing learned is replaced.

The one rule: `data` can go unnamed, the mappings cannot. `sns.scatterplot(asthma,
"smoking_prev_pct", ...)` raises a `TypeError`, because seaborn requires every mapping by name.
That is a good rule; a figure's code should say which column goes where.
:::

## Mapping versus setting {.smaller}

| | **Mapping** | **Setting** |
|---|---|---|
| Drives the property from | a **column** in the data | a **constant** |
| Passed as | a column name, to `x`, `y`, `hue`, `style`, `size` | a value, to `color`, `marker`, `s`, `alpha`, `linewidth`, `linestyle` |
| Example | `hue="metro"` | `color="#003594"` |
| Legend | built automatically | none |

Mappings are seaborn arguments. Settings are matplotlib arguments, which seaborn passes through
to every mark.

::: {.notes}
This is the single most useful distinction in the module, and the R half draws it the same way:
inside `aes()` is mapping, outside is setting.

The test to give the room: does the property change from one county to the next because of the
data? Then it is a mapping, and it takes a column name. Is it the same for every point? Then it
is a setting, and it takes a value.

The pairs of names matter. `hue` maps; `color` sets. `style` maps; `marker` sets. `size` maps;
`s` sets. The mapping names are seaborn's own, and the setting names are matplotlib's, which is
why they do not match. Leave the table up for a moment; the next four slides are examples of it.
:::

## Colour and shape {.smaller}

Both mapped to columns: colour to region, shape to metro status.

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # region and metro per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.6))                 # canvas and one axes
sns.scatterplot(data=joined, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data; smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                hue="region",                              # mapping: region -> colour
                style="metro",                             # mapping: metro -> shape
                s=50, ax=ax)                               # point size; target axes
ax.legend(fontsize=7, bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1),            # move the legend outside ...
          loc="upper left", frameon=False)                 # ... to the right of the axes
plt.tight_layout()                                         # make room for the legend
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
Two different columns now, so colour and shape carry two different variables. The legend grows
two sections, one per mapping.

This is about as much as one scatter should carry. Six colours and two shapes is twelve
combinations, and the eye cannot hold that. Module 6 shows the alternative, which is to split the
groups into separate panels instead of separate colours.

The legend call moves it outside the axes because six regions inside the plotting area cover
the points. `bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1)` means just past the right edge, at the top.
:::

## Size {.smaller}

Mapped to a column (left), and set to a constant (right).

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # population per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

fig, (mapped, fixed) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))   # two panels

sns.scatterplot(data=joined, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data; smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                size="population_2023",                    # MAPPING: population -> marker size
                sizes=(10, 300),                           # smallest and largest marker area
                ax=mapped)                                 # left panel
mapped.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)                   # compact legend
mapped.set_title("size= (mapped)")                         # panel title

sns.scatterplot(data=joined, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # same data and positions
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                s=80,                                      # SETTING: every marker the same area
                ax=fixed)                                  # right panel
fixed.set_title("s= (set)")                                # panel title

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
The left panel is a bubble chart. Philadelphia and Allegheny are the two huge circles; Cameron,
the smallest county at about 4,400 people, is a speck. `sizes=` sets the range of marker areas
the mapping uses.

There is content in the left panel worth one sentence. The three highest-smoking counties —
Forest at 21.8%, Sullivan, and Cameron — are the three smallest counties in the state, the specks
at the far right. That is a preview of a problem Module 6 makes central: small counties produce
the extreme values.

The right panel is a setting. `s=80` makes every point the same size, no legend, nothing in the
data involved.
:::

## Transparency {.smaller}

Set to a constant between 0 and 1. seaborn has **no mapping** for transparency.

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))                 # canvas and one axes
sns.scatterplot(data=asthma, x="smoking_prev_pct",         # data; smoking -> x
                y="asthma_prev_pct",                       # asthma -> y
                s=150,                                     # large markers, so overlaps show
                alpha=0.4,                                 # SETTING: 40% opaque
                ax=ax)                                     # target axes
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

Passing a column name to a setting is an error:

```python
sns.scatterplot(data=asthma, x="smoking_prev_pct", y="asthma_prev_pct",  # data and positions
                alpha="metro")      # TypeError: alpha must be numeric or None, not a string
```

::: {.notes}
Large markers at forty percent opacity, so overlapping counties show up as darker patches. That
is what transparency is for: seeing density where points pile up.

The R half maps alpha to a variable; seaborn simply does not offer that. The error in the
code block is real, verified against the course's seaborn version, and it is the clearest
demonstration of mapping versus setting you will get. `alpha` is a setting. Give it a string
and matplotlib tries to treat `"metro"` as a number.

If someone asks how to fade one group: draw two `scatterplot` calls, one per group, each with its
own `alpha`. That is layering, and Module 6 does it properly.
:::

## Linetype {.smaller}

`sns.lineplot()` maps `style=` to the **dash pattern** of each line.

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

covid = pd.read_csv("data/pa_covid_monthly.csv")           # deaths by county and month
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # population and metro per county
covid["month"] = pd.to_datetime(covid["month"])            # text -> real dates
covid = covid[covid["month"] >= "2021-08-01"]              # keep the reliably reported period

merged = covid.merge(counties[["county", "population_2023", "metro"]],  # attach metro and
                     on="county")                                       # population by county
monthly = (merged.groupby(["month", "metro"], as_index=False)           # one row per month x group
                 [["covid_deaths", "population_2023"]].sum())           # total deaths and people
monthly["per_100k"] = (monthly["covid_deaths"]             # deaths ...
                       / monthly["population_2023"]        # ... per resident ...
                       * 100000)                           # ... per 100,000

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))                   # canvas and one axes
sns.lineplot(data=monthly, x="month", y="per_100k",        # data; time -> x, rate -> y
             hue="metro", style="metro",                   # metro -> colour and dash pattern
             palette={"Metro": "#003594",                  # course colours, by group
                      "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"},              # dark gold for nonmetro
             linewidth=2, ax=ax)                           # SETTING: line width; target axes
ax.set(xlabel="Month",                                     # x-axis label
       ylabel="COVID-19 deaths per 100,000")               # y-axis label with units
ax.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                  # legend title
plt.tight_layout()                                         # keep labels inside the canvas
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
`style=` on a line chart does what it did on a scatter, for lines: one dash pattern per group.
`linewidth=2` is a setting, the same for both lines. To force one fixed pattern on every line,
the setting is `linestyle="--"`.

The filter on the fourth line is not decoration. This file badly undercounts 2020 — one death
statewide for March to June 2020, when the real toll was in the thousands. From mid-2021 it is
reliable. Say that out loud: a file can be real, official, and still wrong for some of its rows.

Read the figure. Nonmetro counties peak first and higher: 44.2 per 100,000 in December 2021,
against 32.9 for metro counties in January 2022. Rates, not counts, so this compares places of
very different size fairly. Module 6 makes the rate-versus-count question its centrepiece.

`pd.to_datetime` matters here: without it the months are text, and the axis would space them
evenly in alphabetical order.
:::

## Default aesthetics {.smaller}

Once a column is mapped, seaborn chooses the rest:

1\. **Axis labels** — the column names: `smoking_prev_pct`

2\. **Legend title** — the column name: `metro`

3\. **Colours** — the `deep` palette, assigned in the order the groups first appear in the data

4\. **Markers and dashes** — a fixed sequence: circle, cross, diamond, …

5\. **Category order** — order of appearance, unless the column is a `pd.Categorical`

Each default has an override: `ax.set()`, `.set_title()` on the legend, `palette=`, `markers=`,
`order=` or a categorical column.

::: {.notes}
This is the list of everything the build-up replaced, stated once in general form. The R half
makes the same point about ggplot2: once a mapping exists, scales and legends follow, and every
one of them can be overridden.

The defaults are guesses made by someone who never saw this figure. They are a good starting
point for exploration and nearly never right for a report. The habit worth building is to read
each one on a draft figure and ask whether it says what you mean.

Number five connects back to the categorical slide. If urbanicity is plain text, seaborn orders
it by first appearance in the file, which is whatever order the rows happen to be in.
:::

## Choosing a figure {.smaller}

The choice of figure follows from two questions: **what type is each variable**, and **how many
variables** are shown.

| Variables | Figure | seaborn | matplotlib |
|---|---|---|---|
| One categorical | Bar of counts | `countplot` | `ax.bar` |
| One numeric | Histogram, boxplot | `histplot`, `boxplot` | `ax.hist`, `ax.boxplot` |
| Numeric by categorical | Boxplot per group | `boxplot` | `ax.boxplot` |
| Two categorical | Grouped bar of counts | `countplot(hue=)` | — |
| Two numeric | Scatter | `scatterplot` | `ax.scatter` |
| Numeric over time | Line | `lineplot` | `ax.plot` |

A line asserts that consecutive points are **connected**. Categories are never joined by a line.

::: {.notes}
This table answers the question students actually have, which is which function to call. It
starts from the data, not from the function list.

The note under the table has teeth. A line between Adams and Allegheny claims the value moved
from one county to the next, which is meaningless; counties have no order. Time and dose have an
order. That is the test for whether a line is allowed.

Module 6 adds rows to this table — densities, violins, statistical bars — but these six cover most
of what a first analysis needs.
:::

## `sns.countplot()`: one and two variables {.smaller}

The height of each bar is the **number of rows** in each category.

```{pyodide}
import micropip                                            # installer for browser packages
await micropip.install("seaborn")                          # fetch seaborn
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import seaborn as sns                                      # statistical figures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # figure and axes

counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # one row per county
levels = (counties.sort_values("urbanicity_code")          # most urban to most rural
                  ["urbanicity"].unique())                 # names in that order
counties["urbanicity"] = pd.Categorical(                   # fix the display order
    counties["urbanicity"], categories=levels, ordered=True)  # column, order, ordered

fig, (one, two) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))    # two panels

sns.countplot(data=counties, y="urbanicity",               # one variable, bars run sideways
              color="#003594", ax=one)                     # SETTING: one colour for all bars
one.set(xlabel="Number of counties", ylabel="")            # labels

sns.countplot(data=counties, x="region",                   # bars per region ...
              hue="metro",                                 # ... split by metro status
              palette={"Metro": "#003594",                 # course colours, by group
                       "Nonmetro": "#8a6400"},             # dark gold for nonmetro
              ax=two)                                      # right panel
two.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Number of counties")            # labels
two.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30)                # tilt long region names
two.get_legend().set_title("Metro status")                 # legend title

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

::: {.notes}
Left panel: one categorical variable, counted. Because urbanicity is now an ordered categorical,
the bars run from Large central metro, just two counties — Philadelphia and Allegheny — down to
Noncore, fourteen. Micropolitan is the largest group at sixteen. Putting it on the y-axis keeps
the long names readable.

Right panel: two categorical variables. `hue=` splits each region's bar by metro status. North
Central is ten nonmetro to four metro; the Southeast is eight to one. That is the shape of
Pennsylvania in one picture: a metropolitan southeast and a rural north.

`countplot` does the counting itself. There is no `y=` column of numbers; seaborn counts rows.
Module 6 calls that a statistical transformation and shows what else hides inside a bar.
:::

## A truncated axis manufactures a difference {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt                            # plotting

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
top5 = asthma.nlargest(5, "asthma_prev_pct")               # the five highest rates

fig, (honest, cut) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.2))  # two panels

honest.bar(top5["county"], top5["asthma_prev_pct"],        # bar per county, height = rate
           color="#003594")                                # fill colour
honest.set_title("Zero baseline")                          # panel title
honest.set_ylabel("Adult asthma (%)")                      # y-axis label

cut.bar(top5["county"], top5["asthma_prev_pct"],           # the same five bars
        color="#8a6400")                                   # fill colour
cut.set_ylim(11.0, 11.7)                                   # start the axis at 11.0, not 0
cut.set_title("Axis starts at 11.0")                       # panel title

for panel in (honest, cut):                                # both panels:
    panel.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45,          # tilt county names
                      labelsize=8)                         # and shrink them

plt.tight_layout()                                         # stop panels overlapping
plt.show()                                                 # render the figure
```

**Identical data. The right panel implies Philadelphia has three times the asthma burden of
Clinton County. The true difference is 0.4 percentage points.**

::: {.callout-important}
## The rule for bars
A bar encodes value by **length**, so its baseline must be zero. Truncating the axis breaks the
correspondence between length and value.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room what the left panel shows first. Someone will say Philadelphia is the worst; someone
sharper will notice the bars are all nearly the same height. That second observation is the real
content.

Then run the right panel and stop talking for a moment. One call to `set_ylim` and the story
changes entirely. Nobody has to be dishonest to produce it — the usual route is an analyst who
zoomed in to see the differences and never zoomed back out.

The rule is specifically about bars. Bars encode by length, so the baseline must be zero. A line
or a scatter encodes by position, and those can start anywhere; the scatters today do not start
at zero and are not misleading.

If someone asks whether the left panel wastes space: yes, and it is worth it. The empty space is
the honest statement that these counties are nearly the same.
:::

# Describing what the figure shows {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

## `.describe()` summarises every numeric column at once {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county

cols = ["asthma_prev_pct", "smoking_prev_pct",             # the three measures
        "obesity_prev_pct"]                                # ... and adult obesity (%)
print(asthma[cols].describe().round(2))                    # eight summaries per column
```

Eight numbers per column: the count, the mean, the standard deviation, the minimum, the three
quartiles, and the maximum.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `count` is the first number to read
It reports **non-missing** values. A count below the number of rows means missing data is
present in that column.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the table across rather than down, because the comparison is the finding. Asthma has a
standard deviation of 0.38. Smoking has 2.32 — six times as wide. Obesity has 2.26.

That single comparison is the cold open expressed as a number: asthma does not vary much across
Pennsylvania counties, while the things that might explain it vary a great deal.

The callout is the habit worth installing. `count` first, every time. Here all three read 67:
CDC PLACES models an estimate for every county, so there is no suppression in this file — unlike
the births file from Module 4.

Mean 10.66 against median 10.60 — the same closeness the histogram's two lines showed. Roughly
symmetric, no tail.
:::

## `.groupby()` and `.agg()` describe each group {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
counties = pd.read_csv("data/pa_counties.csv")             # metro status per county
joined = asthma.merge(counties, on=["county", "fips"])     # one table

summary = joined.groupby("metro").agg(                     # one row per metro group
    counties=("county", "count"),                          # how many counties in the group
    mean_asthma=("asthma_prev_pct", "mean"),               # group mean of asthma
    mean_smoking=("smoking_prev_pct", "mean"),             # group mean of smoking
)                                                          # end of the named aggregations

print(summary.round(2))                                    # two decimals
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The comparison this table makes
Metro and nonmetro counties differ by **0.17** percentage points in asthma prevalence, and by
**2.34** percentage points in smoking prevalence.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the boxplot from earlier as a table, and the numbers say what the overlapping boxes
implied. Asthma: 10.58 metro against 10.75 nonmetro. Smoking: 16.08 against 18.42.

The asthma difference is a sixth of a percentage point and means very little. The smoking
difference is more than two full points. Same table, and one column is carrying nearly all of the
signal — which is what the scatter in the build-up showed with the nonmetro markers sitting to
the right.

Always print the group sizes. A difference in means over four counties and one over thirty-seven
deserve very different confidence, and without the count nobody can tell which they are reading.
:::

## `.corr()` measures how two columns move together {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd                                        # tables

asthma = pd.read_csv("data/pa_asthma_prevalence.csv")      # one row per county
prev = asthma["asthma_prev_pct"]                           # the flat variable

print("smoking vs asthma:",                                # label
      round(asthma["smoking_prev_pct"].corr(prev), 3))     # correlation, 3 decimals
print("obesity vs asthma:",                                # label
      round(asthma["obesity_prev_pct"].corr(prev), 3))     # correlation, 3 decimals
```

A correlation runs from **−1** to **+1**. It reports the strength and direction of a
**straight-line** relationship, and nothing else.

**The answer to the opening question: asthma moves with smoking, at r = +0.659 across 67
counties.**

::: {.callout-important}
## What a correlation cannot establish
It cannot establish cause. It cannot detect a curved relationship. It is distorted by outliers.
**And these are county averages, so it describes counties, not people.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff of the cold open, so slow down. Asthma barely moves between Pennsylvania
counties — under two points across all sixty-seven. Smoking moves across eleven. And they move
together at plus 0.659, the strongest relationship in the course. Obesity comes in at 0.476:
real, weaker, and worth saying so the room does not conclude that everything correlates with
everything.

Now the caveat that carries the most weight. These are county averages. A correlation across
counties describes counties. It does not establish that the people who smoke are the people with
asthma — inferring the second from the first is the ecological fallacy, and they will meet the
name formally elsewhere. Today they meet the caution.

It is consistent with smoking causing asthma, with both sharing upstream causes — income,
occupation, housing — and with combinations of those. The figure earns the relationship. It does
not earn the mechanism. No p-value here, by design.

Module 6 opens by showing how a single point can move this number, which is why the scatter
always comes before the correlation.
:::

## Session outcomes {.smaller}

1\. The **figure/axes model**, and `plt.subplots()` as the entry point to every figure

2\. matplotlib marks: `ax.scatter()`, `ax.hist()`, `ax.boxplot()`, and layers such as `ax.axvline()`

3\. Pairs plots with `pd.plotting.scatter_matrix()`

4\. The **grammar of graphics** in seaborn: data, mappings, and the mark as the function name

5\. **Mapping versus setting**: `hue`, `style`, `size` against `color`, `marker`, `s`, `alpha`

6\. Ordered categories with `pd.Categorical()`; labels with `ax.set()`; colours with `palette=`

7\. **Choosing a figure** from the variable types; `countplot` for counts; **zero baselines for bars**

8\. `.describe()`, grouped `.agg()`, and **`.corr()`** as co-movement, never cause

::: {.callout-tip}
## Preparation for the lab, Thursday 11/12
The lab builds each figure type from this session on the course datasets, and repairs a figure
that misleads without raising an error.
:::

**Module 6 adds seaborn's statistical layers, facets, scales, and themes — and the question of
when a figure of counts is really a figure of population.**

::: {.notes}
The single sentence for the module: a figure is built from data, mappings, and a mark, and every
default it ships with is a guess to be checked.

The second sentence, which transfers beyond this course: the most dangerous figures are not the
broken ones. A figure with no labels is useless and everyone can tell. A bar chart with a
truncated axis is persuasive, and it is wrong, and the code ran perfectly.
